blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — interpret inflammatory-marker results in clinical context
stem: A client has a markedly elevated C-reactive protein (CRP). Which interpretation of this result is most accurate?

options.A: CRP is primarily an infection test; a marked elevation identifies bacterial infection and can replace microbiologic testing when symptoms suggest infection.
options.B: CRP is primarily an autoimmune test; a marked elevation establishes autoimmune disease and makes infection or tissue injury much less likely.
options.C: CRP is a nonspecific inflammatory marker; a marked elevation supports active inflammation but must be interpreted with the clinical picture and other tests.
options.D: CRP is primarily a renal-function marker; a marked elevation indicates reduced glomerular filtration rather than an inflammatory response.

rationale: ARUP Consult states that CRP is a commonly measured inflammatory marker and that inflammatory markers are nonspecific and are not diagnostic for any particular condition. CRP can rise with infection and other inflammatory insults, including tissue injury, and should be interpreted together with the overall clinical picture and other testing. Therefore C is correct. A is incorrect because CRP does not identify a bacterial organism or replace microbiologic testing. B is incorrect because an elevated CRP does not specifically establish autoimmune disease and can rise with infection, trauma, surgery, burns, cancer, and other inflammatory states. D is incorrect because CRP is an inflammatory marker, not a primary measure of glomerular filtration.
educational_objective: Interpret a markedly elevated CRP as evidence supporting active inflammation, while recognizing that CRP is nonspecific and cannot identify a particular disease, pathogen, or organ dysfunction by itself.
source_version_date: Last Literature Review May 2025; Last Update June 2025; live page retrieved 2026-08-26
source_locator: Overview and Laboratory Testing > C-Reactive Protein: inflammation includes infection, trauma, surgery, burns, and cancer; CRP and other common inflammatory markers are nonspecific and not diagnostic for a particular condition; CRP is an early indicator of active systemic inflammation.
source_claim_supported: A markedly elevated CRP supports active inflammation but is nonspecific and must be interpreted with the clinical picture and other diagnostic information.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential, printed p.13/PDF p.17: perform focused assessments; recognize trends and changes in client condition; monitor the results of diagnostic testing and intervene as needed.
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four alternatives to remove the correct-answer length cue and keep each option within the same laboratory-interpretation construct. The revised key preserves the supported nonspecificity of CRP without adding an unsupported diagnostic threshold or disease-specific claim.

audit_findings.stem: PASS — asks only for interpretation of a markedly elevated CRP and does not require an unstated numeric threshold or diagnosis.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS as distractor — plausible infection anchoring, but CRP is nonspecific and cannot identify a bacterial organism or replace diagnostic testing.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — plausible autoimmune anchoring, but ARUP lists multiple infectious and noninfectious inflammatory causes of CRP elevation.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS — directly reflects ARUP guidance that CRP is a nonspecific marker of active inflammation interpreted with the clinical picture and other tests.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — plausible laboratory-category error, but CRP is not a renal-filtration marker.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — only C preserves the supported nonspecific inflammatory interpretation without assigning an unsupported specific etiology.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — A and B overdiagnose a specific cause; D assigns the wrong physiologic construct.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — correct option is no longer uniquely longest; all alternatives are parallel interpretation statements without distractor-only absolute wording.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — interpretation of a diagnostic laboratory result aligns directly with Reduction of Risk Potential.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether a markedly elevated CRP could reasonably imply bacterial infection or autoimmune disease. Current ARUP guidance explicitly describes CRP as nonspecific and not diagnostic for any particular condition, leaving C uniquely best.
